tagline: From Patuxent River landings to the defense of Baltimore Harbor
intro: The Star-Spangled Banner Scenic Byway links Southern Maryland towns, sites near Washington and Baltimore’s harbor, extending from Hollywood to Edgemere. Visit Maryland presents this 106-mile drive as a way to trace the War of 1812 through the Chesapeake landscape and gives a driving time of three to four hours. The route combines state roads, the Capital Beltway and the Baltimore-Washington Parkway before reaching Baltimore’s streets.

At Aquasco, roads linking scattered tobacco plantations were established in the eighteenth century. In the early nineteenth century, the village of Woodville began to form along this agricultural network. The journey’s historical thread is the campaign of 1814, when British forces advanced up the Patuxent and landed at Benedict to march on Washington. Joshua Barney’s Chesapeake Flotilla had fought several inconclusive naval engagements before he ordered its destruction on August 22. Its men then fought ashore in the defense of Washington and Baltimore.

Begin at Sotterley above the Patuxent, then cross to Solomons and continue through St. Leonard to Benedict. Head north through Upper Marlboro and Bladensburg, then take the parkway toward Fort McHenry in Baltimore. The itinerary continues to the North Point peninsula and the Edgemere end of the byway.

moments.title: Sotterley
moments.text: During the War of 1812, more than 50 people enslaved at Sotterley claimed freedom by fleeing to the British. Peregrine Young, Ignatius Seale, Joseph Wood and James Bowie were among those who secretly met with British forces to plan an emancipation movement. The plantation overlooking the Patuxent was also raided by the British. Descendants of Sotterley’s enslaved population help manage and interpret the site. The surviving landscape includes an original cabin for enslaved people, a customs warehouse and a corn crib. The sawn-log cabin dates to circa 1830, after the wartime escapes.
moments.notice: The plantation house overlooks the Patuxent River; an original cabin for enslaved people survives on the property.

moments.title: Benedict
moments.text: Benedict’s position on the Patuxent made it a landing place for the British invasion of Washington. General Robert Ross’s army landed here on August 18, 1814, then marched inland and defeated a larger American force at Bladensburg before burning the capital. British troops returned to Benedict to embark again after the attack. The town began as a fishing village in the late seventeenth century. Beside it, the half-mile Benedict Bridge carries MD 231 across the Patuxent between Charles and Calvert counties. During the Civil War, Benedict became the site of Camp Stanton, where the 19th Regiment of the United States Colored Troops formed in December 1863.

moments.title: Fort McHenry
moments.text: The flag that inspired Francis Scott Key replaced a smaller one. A 17-by-25-foot storm flag flew during the British bombardment; early on September 14, 1814, a 30-by-42-foot garrison flag took its place. Key watched from a truce ship after negotiating an American prisoner’s release, and the sight prompted his poem. The star-shaped fort’s ramparts are part of the visitor experience. Mary Pickersgill sewed the large flag with African-American household members including Grace Wisher. The historic flag itself is displayed at the National Museum of American History. That flag carries fifteen stars and fifteen stripes.
